t: Choose Numbers From Two Arrays in Range — Sliding-Balance DP
o: A range [l, r] is balanced when you can pick one number per index from nums1 or nums2 so that the picked sums are equal — equivalently, when the running difference (sum picked from nums1) − (sum picked from nums2) can be driven to 0. In example 1 ([1,2,5] vs [2,6,3]) three (range, choice) pairs qualify: [0,1] via nums2[0] + nums1[1] (2 = 2), and two different assignments for [0,2], namely 1 + 5 = 6 vs nums2[1] and 1 + 2 = 3 vs nums2[2]. Example 2 shows zeros matter: [0,0] and [1,1] balance trivially because picking a 0 keeps both sums equal. With n ≤ 100 and values ≤ 100 the difference stays within ±10⁴, so carrying a map from difference → number of choice combinations for ranges ending at the current index costs O(n·10⁴) work — comfortably fast.
k: Track a single signed balance, sum picked from nums1 minus sum picked from nums2; balanced ⇔ balance = 0.
Extend every range ending at r − 1 to r in O(1) per state: balance += nums1[r] or balance −= nums2[r].
Ranges with identical endpoints but different pick patterns count separately, so tally assignments (map values), not just windows.

a.n: Approach 1: Hash Map DP Over Ranges Ending at Each Index
a.i: Sweep r left to right keeping dp[balance] = number of choice combinations over all ranges [l, r]. Starting a fresh range at r contributes one combination at +nums1[r] and one at −nums2[r]; every previous state spawns those same two successors. After processing r, add dp[0] to the answer.
s: Initialize an empty hash map dp and ans = 0.
For each index r with a = nums1[r], b = nums2[r]: create ndp; seed ndp[a] += 1 and ndp[−b] += 1.
For each (balance, ways) in dp: ndp[balance + a] += ways and ndp[balance − b] += ways, all mod 10⁹ + 7.
ans += ndp[0]; replace dp with ndp.
a.t: O(n · S) where S ≤ 20001 distinct balances — each of the n steps copies every state twice.
a.sp: O(S) — only two balance maps coexist.

a.i: Replace hashing with direct indexing: every balance provably lies in [−10000, 10000] because each of the ≤ 100 picks changes it by at most 100. An array of size 20001 shifted by offset 10000 gives constant-time writes, no hashing overhead, and cache-friendly sweeps — the same recurrence with better constants.
s: Allocate arrays dp and ndp of size 20001 with offset OFF = 10000; clear dp initially.
Per index r with a = nums1[r], b = nums2[r]: zero ndp; scatter each nonzero dp[j] into j + a and j − b when in range.
Seed ndp[OFF + a] += 1 and ndp[OFF − b] += 1.
Add ndp[OFF] (balance 0) to the answer; swap dp and ndp.
a.t: O(n · Σvalues) ≈ O(100 · 20001) — a full array sweep per index regardless of how many balances are alive.

w: Present the hash-map version first because the extend-every-range-by-one-index story is clearest there, then note that bounded values let you flatten it into an array. The classic bug is counting windows instead of assignments — example 1's duplicate [0,2] exists precisely because different pick patterns count separately. Watch zeros: picking 0 from either array leaves the balance unchanged and doubles branching without progress. Follow-ups: weight each balanced range by its length, or allow negative values (the offset simply grows to Σ|values|).
